name: Coatlán Zapotec

tone_statements.citation: Benton, Joseph P. 2012. Proto-Zapotec Phonology. Draft manuscript (posted 'as is' without peer review; 'revised over several years of research'), 141 pp. SIL Language & Culture Archives, entry 77274 (file, 873 KB).
tone_statements.quote: Rather than give examples of vowel length from Coatlán, of which there are many, I consider that it will suffice to show the co-occurrence of length with tone. As can be expected, the number of cases in which length co-occurs with contour tones (especially falling) is notably greater than with with non-contour tones. The data source for the following statistics is Robinson (1963). Coatlán Tone Number of occurrences of length 1 2 2 2 3 2 31 6 13 19 23 30 … "1" is the highest tone, and "4" is the lowest.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 72-73, sec. 3.2 Tone (tone and vowel length); last sentence: Appendix A intro, p. 109
tone_statements.summary: Comparative Proto-Zapotec study; cites Santa Maria Coatlan forms (Robinson's 1963 field notes) with six numbered tones: levels 1, 2, 3 (1 = highest), contours 31, 13, 23; length favours falling tones.

tone_statements.quote: Contrastive glottalization is excluded here as it is historically not part of the tonal system, though it has become so in modern Coatec. … Figure 2 shows the tonal correspondences found between the San Baltazar Loxicha (SBalL) and Coatlán dialects of Coatec and the San Agustín Mixtepec (SAM), San Agustín Loxicha (SAL), and San Bartolomé Loxicha (SBarL) dialects of Miahuatec. … Falling tones in the varieties considered seem to have developed recently from high tone (Coatec) and low tone (SBarL) and there are no mid tones in the varieties examined.

tone_statements.quote: En el coateco el tono alto tiene una realización alto-nivel en algunos entornos pero alto-descendente en otros. Mayormente el tono alto en el coateco se encuentra en sílabas átonas y en palabras prestadas del español. [...] Cuadro 6. tone_statements.citation: Beam de Azcona, Rosemary G. 2004. A Coatlán-Loxicha Zapotec grammar (Mexico). PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley; and her Southern Zapotec comparative work (e.g. 2008 map and subgrouping cited by Leander).
tone_statements.quote: Polysyllabic words in CLZ have final stress. Final syllables tend to be heavy CVC syllables although they may be light CV syllables. Pre-tonic syllables tend to be light (C)V syllables although they may be heavy (C)VC syllables. Unstressed syllables can only take high tone while stressed syllables can take any tone, although high tone is the least common of the five tones in stressed syllables. [...] In sum, an unstressed syllable is any non-final syllable with high tone. All final syllables are stressed and the prominence which is stress can be attained either by a non-high tone or by syllable weight or both.

sources.citation: Beam de Azcona, Rosemary G. 2023. 'The tonal morphology of the potential in Coatec Zapotec (Di'zhke'): implications for early Zapotecan tone, *ʔ, and verb classes through internal and comparative reconstruction'. Journal of Historical Linguistics (author's last preprint).
sources.quote: 'Every phonological word in Coatec has a single prominent syllable, which bears one of these five tones. Other than loanwords (e.g., /eskoˈpét/ 'shotgun') and compounds (e.g., /jit͡ʃèk/ ...), most words are monosyllabic due to the loss of unstressed vowels'; pre-tonic syllables occur mostly in compounds and loans with tonal contrasts neutralized.
sources.locator: sec. 2 (preprint text around ex. (8)) and sec. 4.1.1
sources.note: Most recent statement by the same author: one prominent syllable per phonological word, final in loans/compounds; independent confirmation 19 years after the grammar.
sources.venue: Journal of Historical Linguistics (author's last preprint)
